title: Food, drink and the accusative
objectives: I can order food and drink in a café with 'Мо́жна...?' and 'Мені́..., будь ла́ска', and ask for the bill.
I can say what I and other people want, eat, drink and see, with the present of 'хоті́ти', 'ї́сти', 'пи́ти' and 'ба́чити'.
I can put a noun and its adjective into the accusative singular, choosing the ending by gender and, for masculine nouns, by whether the noun names a living being.
I can use the accusative pronouns 'мене́', 'тебе́', 'його́', 'її́', 'нас', 'вас' and 'їх', and explain the phrase 'Як тебе́ зва́ти?'.
I can wish someone a good meal with 'Смачно́го!' and say what it means word for word.

vocabulary.note: Present 'хо́чу', 'хо́чеш', 'вони́ хо́чуть'. The stem 'хот-' becomes 'хоч-' in every present form, with the endings of the first conjugation and the stress on the first syllable. It takes a noun in the accusative or an infinitive.
Irregular present: 'їм', 'їси́', 'їсть', 'їмо́', 'їсте́', 'їдя́ть'. The 'вони́' form keeps the 'д' of the old stem 'їд-'.
Present 'п’ю', 'п’єш', 'вони́ п’ють'. The 'и' of the infinitive drops out, and the apostrophe keeps the 'п' hard before the [j] of the ending.
Second conjugation: 'ба́чу', 'ба́чиш', 'вони́ ба́чать'. After 'ч' the endings are '-у' and '-ать', not '-ю' and '-ять', because 'ч' is never fully soft.

vocabulary.source: to study, to learn a subject
vocabulary.note: Present like 'чита́ти': 'вивча́ю', 'вивча́єш'. The thing studied is its direct object, in the accusative. The second 'в', before 'ч', is said [w].
Written with a small letter, like every adjective of nationality. The 'с' is soft before the soft sign. Feminine 'украї́нська', feminine accusative 'украї́нську'.
It names a thing, so its accusative is also 'суп'.
Its accusative is also 'сала́т'.

vocabulary.part_of_speech: masculine noun, cited in the plural
vocabulary.note: One dumpling is 'варе́ник'. They are eaten many at a time, so the plural is the usual form, and as a plural that names things it keeps the same form in the accusative.

A mass noun, a noun for a substance that is not counted one by one: Ukrainian uses the singular for potatoes as food, as English does for 'rice'. Accusative 'карто́плю'; the 'л' is soft before both 'я' and 'ю'.
Accusative 'ковбасу́'. The 'в' before 'б' is said [w].
Accusative 'ча́шку'.

example.source: May I have a cup, please?

vocabulary.note: Accusative 'скля́нку'. The 'л' is soft before 'я'.

example.source: The glass is here, and the cup is there.

vocabulary.note: A borrowed noun that never changes form. The 'н' is soft before 'ю'.
Other forms use the stem 'раху́нк-', but the accusative is the same as the nominative, because a bill is a thing.
Four syllables: 'і' and 'а' are two separate vowels, not one sound, and the stress is on the last. A waiter is a person, so the accusative is 'офіціа́нта'.
Accusative 'офіціа́нтку'.
Feminine 'смачна́', neuter 'смачне́', plural 'смачні́'. The stress stays on the ending in every form, as in the feminine accusative 'смачну́'.
The whole predicate of a sentence that has no subject. With a noun in the accusative it asks politely for that thing.

vocabulary.source: it is tasty, it is delicious
vocabulary.note: Made from 'смачни́й'. It says how food tastes in a sentence with no subject, while 'Борщ смачни́й.' names the dish as the subject.
The genitive of 'смачни́й', said alone as a wish when food is served or someone starts to eat. The answer is 'Дя́кую!'.

dialogues.title: Lunch at Andrii's café
dialogues.context: Oksana and Sam have lunch at the café of Andrii, who knows them both and brings them the menu. The two friends say 'ти' to each other and 'ви' to Andrii, and Andrii says 'ви' to the two of them.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: До́брий день! Меню́, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: Good afternoon! Here is the menu.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Дя́кую, па́не Андрі́ю. Се́ме, що ти хо́чеш?
lines.source: Thank you, Mr. Andrii. Sam, what would you like?
lines.source_literal: I-thank, sir Andrii. Sam, what you want?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я хо́чу борщ. Я ду́же люблю́ борщ.
lines.source: I want borscht. I really love borscht.
lines.source_literal: I want borscht. I very love borscht.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А я хо́чу варе́ники й сала́т.
lines.source: And I want varenyky and a salad.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: До́бре. А що ви хо́чете пи́ти?
lines.source: Fine. And what would you like to drink?
lines.source_literal: well. and what you want to-drink?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мо́жна ка́ву з молоко́м, будь ла́ска?
lines.source: Can I have a coffee with milk, please?
lines.source_literal: possible coffee with milk, be kindness?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А мені́ чай із цу́кром, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: And tea with sugar for me, please.
lines.source_literal: and to-me tea with sugar, be kindness.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Ка́ву з молоко́м і чай із цу́кром. А во́ду?
lines.source: A coffee with milk and a tea with sugar. And water?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: Yes, please.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Борщ, варе́ники й сала́т. Смачно́го!
lines.source: Borscht, varenyky and salad. Enjoy your meal!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! Борщ ду́же смачни́й.
lines.source: Thank you! The borscht is very tasty.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: І варе́ники ду́же смачні́! Ду́же смачно́, па́не Андрі́ю!
lines.source: And the varenyky are very tasty! It is delicious, Mr. Andrii!
lines.source_literal: and varenyky very tasty! very tasty, sir Andrii!

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Дя́кую! Ду́же приє́мно.
lines.source: Thank you! That is very nice to hear.

dialogues.title: What are we eating?
dialogues.context: Taras and his sister Olena are at home in the evening and decide what to eat. As brother and sister they say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Оле́но, я хо́чу ї́сти. А ти?
lines.source: Olena, I am hungry. Are you?
lines.source_literal: Olena, I want to-eat. and you?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: І я. Що тут є?
lines.source: Me too. What do we have here?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Я ба́чу ковбасу́, сир і хліб.
lines.source: I see sausage, cheese and bread.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ковбасу́? Ні, я хо́чу суп.
lines.source: Sausage? No, I want soup.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тут є борщ. Ма́ма ро́бить ду́же смачни́й борщ.
lines.source: There is borscht here. Mom makes very tasty borscht.
lines.source_literal: here there-is borscht. mom makes very tasty borscht.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Борщ я ду́же люблю́! І я хо́чу карто́плю.
lines.source: I really love borscht! And I want potatoes.
lines.source_literal: borscht I very love! and I want potatoes.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре. Я їм борщ і хліб. А що ми п’ємо́?
lines.source: Fine. I am having borscht and bread. And what are we drinking?
lines.source_literal: well. I eat borscht and bread. and what we drink?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Я п’ю во́ду. А ти? Сік чи чай?
lines.source: I am drinking water. And you? Juice or tea?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Чай. Де ча́шка?
lines.source: Tea. Where is the cup?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ча́шка там. Тара́се, ти ба́чиш кота́?
lines.source: The cup is over there. Taras, do you see the cat?
lines.source_literal: cup there. Taras, you see cat?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ба́чу. Він хо́че ковбасу́!
lines.source: I do. He wants the sausage!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А ми хо́чемо борщ. Смачно́го, Тара́се!
lines.source: And we want borscht. Enjoy your meal, Taras!
lines.source_literal: and we want borscht. of-tasty, Taras!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Дя́кую, Оле́но! Смачно́го!
lines.source: Thank you, Olena! Enjoy your meal!

dialogues.title: The bill, please
dialogues.context: Sam, Oksana and Taras have dinner at Andrii's café. Bohdan, a waiter there, serves them; they say 'ви' to him, and the three friends say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Борщ, варе́ники й ка́ва, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: Borscht, varenyky and coffee. Here you are.
lines.source_literal: borscht, varenyky and coffee, be kindness.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! Смачно́го, дру́зі!
lines.source: Thank you! Enjoy your meal, friends!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Дя́кую, Се́ме! Смачно́го!
lines.source: Thank you, Sam! Enjoy your meal!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Се́ме, ти зна́єш Богда́на?
lines.source: Sam, do you know Bohdan?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, я його́ зна́ю. А Окса́на зна́є його́ бра́та.
lines.source: Yes, I know him. And Oksana knows his brother.
lines.source_literal: yes, I him know. and Oksana knows his brother.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, я зна́ю його́ бра́та. Він студе́нт.
lines.source: Yes, I know his brother. He is a student.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Окса́но, ти ба́чиш Андрі́я? Він там, і він ба́чить нас.
lines.source: Oksana, do you see Andrii? He is over there, and he sees us.
lines.source_literal: Oksana, you see Andrii? he there, and he sees us.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ба́чу. До́брий ве́чір, па́не Андрі́ю!
lines.source: I do. Good evening, Mr. Andrii!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ви́бачте! Мо́жна раху́нок, будь ла́ска?
lines.source: Excuse me! Can I have the check, please?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Так, за́раз.
lines.source: Yes, right away.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Ваш раху́нок, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: Here is your check.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! Борщ ду́же смачни́й. До поба́чення!
lines.source: Thank you! The borscht is very tasty. Goodbye!
lines.source_literal: I-thank! borscht very tasty. until seeing!

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Дя́кую! До поба́чення!
lines.source: Thank you! Goodbye!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the first four units. A few of them show those rules at work in ways worth looking at closely.

The apostrophe appears inside a verb. The infinitive 'пи́ти' has the root 'пи-'. In the present the 'и' drops out and each ending begins with the sound [j]: 'п’ю', 'п’єш', 'п’є', 'п’ємо́', 'п’єте́', 'п’ють'. After a consonant, 'ю' and 'є' normally soften it and lose their [j], but 'п' is never fully soft. The apostrophe after 'п' shows exactly this: the 'п' stays hard and the [j] is sounded. 'П’ю' is one syllable, [pju], close to English 'pew'.

The verb 'ї́сти' shows the letter 'ї', which is always [ji] and never softens the sound before it: 'ї́сти' [ˈjistɪ], 'їм' [jim], 'їси́' [jiˈsɪ]. Its 'вони́' form 'їдя́ть' brings back a 'д' that the other forms lost. That 'д' is soft before 'я', said with the middle of the tongue raised, and 'я' after a consonant gives [ɑ], so the word is [jiˈdʲɑtʲ]. In 'їсть' the soft sign softens the 'т', and the 'с' before a soft 'т' is said soft as well: [jisʲtʲ].

The verb 'хоті́ти' shows an alternation, a sound inside the root that changes between forms of the same word, like the 'і' and 'о' of 'кіт' and 'кота́'. Its 'т' becomes 'ч' in every present form, and the stress moves from the second syllable to the first: 'хоті́ти', 'хо́чу', 'хо́чеш'. Learn the 'я' and 'ти' forms together with the infinitive, as with every verb whose present cannot be built from the infinitive.

The letter 'в' follows the rule of the first unit: [ʋ] before a vowel, and [w], as in 'cow', at the end of a syllable before a consonant.

- 'ковбаса́' is [kɔwbɑˈsɑ].
- 'вивча́ти' is [ʋɪwˈt͡ʃɑtɪ], with both sounds in one word.

Soft consonants appear before 'я', 'ю', 'і' and the soft sign.

- The 'л' of 'карто́пля' and 'скля́нка' is soft before 'я', and it stays soft in 'карто́плю', because 'ю' softens too.
- The 'н' of 'меню́' is soft before 'ю'.
- The 'ц' of 'офіціа́нт' is soft before 'і', and the 'і' and 'а' after it are two vowels in two syllables, so the word has four syllables.
- The 'с' of 'украї́нський' is soft before the soft sign, and the 'к' after it is hard.

The adjective ending '-ого' in 'смачно́го' and 'ново́го' is said as it is written, [ɔɦɔ], with the voiced 'г' [ɦ] of the second unit.

Finally, the stress. Some nouns stressed on the last syllable move the stress to the first syllable in the accusative: 'вода́', 'во́ду'; 'рука́', 'ру́ку'; 'нога́', 'но́гу'; 'голова́', 'го́лову'. Others keep it on the ending: 'сестра́', 'сестру́'; 'ковбаса́', 'ковбасу́'. No rule predicts which, so learn the stress of each form as the tables show it. The adjective 'смачни́й' keeps its stress on the ending in every form: 'смачна́', 'смачну́', 'смачно́го'.

grammar.title: The accusative: the case of the direct object
grammar.explanation:
A direct object is the person or thing that an action is done to: in 'Oksana is drinking coffee', Oksana is the subject and the coffee is the direct object. English shows which is which by word order, with the subject before the verb and the object after it. Ukrainian shows it with the ending. The direct object goes into the accusative, 'знахі́дний відмі́нок', the case whose questions are 'кого́?' for people and animals and 'що?' for things: 'Окса́на п’є ка́ву.' The '-у' of 'ка́ву' marks the coffee as what is drunk.

Because the ending carries the job, the words can move without changing who does what. 'Ка́ву п’є Окса́на.' still means that Oksana is drinking the coffee; putting 'Окса́на' last makes her the new information, as English does with 'It is Oksana who is drinking the coffee'. In the same way 'Окса́ну ба́чить Тара́с.' means that Taras sees Oksana: 'Окса́ну' can only be the object, and 'Тара́с' can only be the subject.

Most verbs of this unit and the earlier units take a direct object in the accusative: 'чита́ти', 'писа́ти', 'зна́ти', 'люби́ти', 'роби́ти', 'слу́хати', 'вивча́ти', 'хоті́ти', 'ї́сти', 'пи́ти' and 'ба́чити'. The ending depends on the gender of the noun, and for masculine nouns also on whether the noun names a living being.

- Feminine nouns in '-а' change it to '-у': 'ка́ва', 'ка́ву'; 'ри́ба', 'ри́бу'; 'сестра́', 'сестру́'; 'Окса́на', 'Окса́ну'.
- Feminine nouns in '-я' change it to '-ю': 'карто́пля', 'карто́плю'; 'пі́сня', 'пі́сню'; 'Со́фія', 'Со́фію'.
- Feminine nouns that end in a consonant, often written with the soft sign, do not change: 'сіль', 'о́сінь'.
- Neuter nouns do not change: 'молоко́', 'м’я́со', 'я́блуко', 'меню́'.
- Masculine nouns that name things do not change: 'суп', 'хліб', 'борщ', 'сир', 'чай', 'раху́нок'.
- Masculine nouns that name people or animals add '-а' after a hard consonant and '-я' after a soft consonant or 'й': 'брат', 'бра́та'; 'друг', 'дру́га'; 'Тара́с', 'Тара́са'; 'Сем', 'Се́ма'; 'кіт', 'кота́'; 'вчи́тель', 'вчи́теля'; 'Андрі́й', 'Андрі́я'.
- Plural nouns that name things do not change: 'варе́ники', 'я́блука'. Plural nouns that name people take another form, which comes with the plural cases in A2.

Grammar calls a noun that names a person or an animal animate, and any other noun inanimate. In the singular only masculine nouns are affected by the difference, and the reason is old. Masculine nouns once had the same form for subject and object. That did no harm with things, since soup does not eat anyone, but a sentence with two men in it could not show who did what to whom. The language solved this by giving an animate masculine object the form of another case, the genitive, which a later unit teaches; that is where the '-а' of 'бра́та' comes from. Feminine nouns never had the problem, because their '-у' already differs from their '-а', so 'сестру́' and 'ка́ву' take the same ending.

In 'кіт', 'кота́' the alternation of the fifth unit is at work: the ending '-а' opens the syllable, and the 'і' of the closed syllable returns to 'о'. Masculine nouns with other endings change by their ending: 'та́то' ends in '-о' and becomes 'та́та', like 'брат', while 'Мико́ла', a man's name in '-а', changes like 'ма́ма', giving 'Мико́лу'. Nouns that never change form, such as 'кафе́', 'меню́' and 'па́ні', stay as they are in the accusative too.

examples.source: It is Oksana who is drinking the coffee.

grammar.title: Adjectives and possessives in the accusative
grammar.explanation:
An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case, so when the noun goes into the accusative, the adjective goes with it. The adjective follows the noun's rule exactly: it changes where the noun changes and stays the same where the noun stays the same.

- With a feminine noun, the hard ending '-а' becomes '-у' and the soft ending '-я' becomes '-ю': 'смачна́ ка́ва', 'смачну́ ка́ву'; 'нова́ кни́га', 'нову́ кни́гу'; 'си́ня ру́чка', 'си́ню ру́чку'.
- With a masculine noun that names a thing, and with a neuter noun, nothing changes: 'смачни́й суп', 'смачне́ м’я́со', 'нове́ вікно́'.
- With a masculine noun that names a person or an animal, the hard ending '-ий' becomes '-ого' and the soft ending '-ій' becomes '-ього': 'нови́й друг', 'ново́го дру́га'; 'вели́кий кіт', 'вели́кого кота́'; 'стари́й офіціа́нт', 'старо́го офіціа́нта'; 'сере́дній брат', the middle brother, 'сере́днього бра́та'.
- With a plural noun that names things, nothing changes: 'смачні́ варе́ники'.

Most adjectives keep their stress on the same syllable in every form: 'вели́кий', 'вели́ку', 'вели́кого'. Adjectives stressed on the ending, such as 'нови́й', 'стари́й', 'мали́й' and 'смачни́й', keep it on the ending, which in '-ого' means the first 'о': 'ново́го', 'старо́го', 'мало́го', 'смачно́го'.

The possessive pronouns 'мій', 'твій', 'наш' and 'ваш' agree in the same way.

- Feminine: 'моя́' becomes 'мою́', 'твоя́' becomes 'твою́', 'на́ша' becomes 'на́шу', 'ва́ша' becomes 'ва́шу'.
- Masculine, for a person or an animal: 'мій' becomes 'мого́', 'твій' becomes 'твого́', 'наш' becomes 'на́шого', 'ваш' becomes 'ва́шого'.
- Masculine for a thing, and neuter: no change, as in 'мій суп' and 'моє́ я́блуко'.

The question word 'яки́й' does the same: 'Яку́ ка́ву ти хо́чеш?' asks which coffee you want, and 'Яко́го дру́га ти ба́чиш?' asks which friend you see.

The words 'його́', 'її́' and 'їх', meaning 'his', 'her' and 'their', never change, because they do not agree with the noun as the possessive pronouns do: they are the genitive forms of 'він', 'вона́' and 'вони́', literally 'of-him', 'of-her' and 'of-them'. So 'його́ сестра́' becomes 'його́ сестру́', and only the noun changes.

grammar.title: Personal pronouns in the accusative
grammar.explanation:
Pronouns have cases too. English keeps a trace of this: 'I' becomes 'me', 'he' becomes 'him', 'she' becomes 'her', 'we' becomes 'us' and 'they' becomes 'them' when they are objects, and only 'you' and 'it' stay the same. Ukrainian changes every personal pronoun.

- 'я' becomes 'мене́'.
- 'ти' becomes 'тебе́'.
- 'він' and 'воно́' become 'його́'.
- 'вона́' becomes 'її́'.
- 'ми' becomes 'нас'.
- 'ви' becomes 'вас'.
- 'вони́' becomes 'їх'.

Because 'він', 'вона́' and 'воно́' also mean 'it', chosen by the gender of the noun, the accusative follows the gender of the thing: 'Де ка́ва? Я її́ ба́чу.' is 'Where is the coffee? I see it.', and 'Борщ? Я його́ ду́же люблю́.' is 'Borscht? I love it.'

An object pronoun can stand after the verb, as in English, or before it: 'Я ба́чу тебе́.' and 'Я тебе́ ба́чу.' are both correct and both common. After the verb the pronoun sits in the last place, where new information goes, so it carries a little more weight.

The forms 'його́', 'її́' and 'їх' are also the words for 'his', 'her' and 'their' met with the possessives. A noun right after the form shows which one is meant. 'Я ба́чу її́.' is 'I see her', but 'Я ба́чу її́ бра́та.' is 'I see her brother': there 'її́' says whose brother it is, and 'бра́та' is the object.

The accusative pronouns explain two phrases of the greetings unit. 'Зва́ти' is the infinitive 'to call', and these sentences have no subject. 'Мене́ зва́ти Сем.' is literally 'me to-call Sam', and 'Як тебе́ зва́ти?' is literally 'how you to-call?': the person being named stands in the accusative as the object of the calling. 'Як вас зва́ти?' asks politely, and 'Як його́ зва́ти?' and 'Як її́ зва́ти?' ask the name of someone else.

examples.target: Де Окса́на й Тара́с? Я їх не ба́чу.
examples.source: Where are Oksana and Taras? I do not see them.
examples.source_literal: where Oksana and Taras? I them not see.

grammar.title: Wanting, eating, drinking and seeing: the verbs of this unit
grammar.explanation:
The verbs of this unit are among the most common in the language, and the most common verbs are the ones most likely to keep old, irregular forms, as English 'to be' keeps 'am', 'is' and 'are'. Three of them cannot be built from the infinitive with the rules of the previous unit, so learn their present forms whole.

'Хоті́ти', to want, has the stem 'хоч-' in every present form, with the endings of the first conjugation and the stress on the first syllable: 'хо́чу', 'хо́чеш', 'хо́че', 'хо́чемо', 'хо́чете', 'хо́чуть'.

'Ї́сти', to eat, has endings of its own: 'їм', 'їси́', 'їсть', 'їмо́', 'їсте́', 'їдя́ть'. The '-м' of 'їм' is an ending so old that only a handful of Ukrainian verbs keep it, the way English keeps an old '-m' in 'am'. The 'вони́' form shows the 'д' of the old stem 'їд-'. Watch the stress: 'їмо́' and 'їсте́' are stressed on the ending, while the infinitive 'ї́сти' is stressed on its first syllable and ends in 'и'.

'Пи́ти', to drink, drops the 'и' of its root and takes the first conjugation endings that follow a vowel, as in 'чита́ю': 'п’ю', 'п’єш', 'п’є', 'п’ємо́', 'п’єте́', 'п’ють'.

The other two new verbs are regular.

- 'Ба́чити', to see, follows the second conjugation: 'ба́чу', 'ба́чиш', 'ба́чить', 'ба́чимо', 'ба́чите', 'ба́чать'. After 'ч' the endings are '-у' and '-ать', not '-ю' and '-ять', because 'ч' is never fully soft.
- 'Вивча́ти', to study a subject, follows the first conjugation like 'чита́ти': 'вивча́ю', 'вивча́єш', 'вивча́ють'.

All five take a direct object in the accusative. 'Хоті́ти' can also take an infinitive, just as 'люби́ти' can. 'Я хо́чу ї́сти.' is literally 'I want to-eat', and it is the everyday way to say 'I am hungry'; 'Я хо́чу пи́ти.' says 'I am thirsty'. As with every verb, one present form covers both 'I eat' and 'I am eating': 'Що ти їси́?' asks what you eat or what you are eating, and the situation decides.

Among friends 'Я хо́чу...' is a normal way to say what you would like. To a waiter or in a shop it sounds blunt, and the phrases of the next note are used instead.

grammar.title: Ordering: 'Мо́жна...?', 'Мені́..., будь ла́ска' and 'Смачно́го!'
grammar.explanation:
A predicative word is a word that forms the whole predicate of a sentence with no grammatical subject. Most predicative words end in '-о' and look like adverbs, but they are not adverbs: an adverb describes an action, as 'до́бре' does in 'Я до́бре розумі́ю.', while a predicative word is itself what the sentence states. You met one in the greetings unit: 'Ду́же приє́мно.' is literally 'very pleasant', a statement with no subject. This unit adds two.

- 'Мо́жна' says that something is allowed or possible.
- 'Смачно́' says that food tastes good: 'Ду́же смачно́!' is 'It is delicious!'.

'Мо́жна' with a noun is the usual polite way to ask for something. 'Мо́жна ка́ву?', literally 'possible coffee?', means 'Can I have a coffee?'. The noun is in the accusative because it is the object of a giving that is understood but not said. 'Мо́жна?' alone asks 'May I?', for example before taking a free chair.

The other common way to order is 'Мені́..., будь ла́ска'. 'Мені́ борщ, будь ла́ска.' is literally 'to-me borscht, be kindness', and means 'Borscht for me, please.' 'Мені́' is a form of 'я' in the dative, the case of the person something is given to, which comes in A2; for now the phrase is learned whole. The thing ordered is again in the accusative: 'Мені́ ка́ву, будь ла́ска.' When a second person orders, 'А мені́...' says 'and for me...'.

The phrases 'ка́ва з молоко́м' and 'чай із цу́кром' from the stress unit keep their form inside an order. Only the main noun goes into the accusative, as in 'Мені́ ка́ву з молоко́м.' The words 'молоко́м' and 'цу́кром' are in the instrumental, the case used after 'з' when it means 'with', which also comes in A2.

'Смачно́го!' is the genitive of 'смачни́й', literally 'of-tasty'. A wish in Ukrainian puts what is wished in the genitive, and here the words for 'I wish you' and the noun the adjective describes are left out, so only the adjective remains. It is said when food is served and when someone sits down to eat, and the answer is 'Дя́кую!'.

A meal in a café also uses phrases you already know.

- 'Ви́бачте!' catches the waiter's attention.
- 'Будь ла́ска.' also means 'Here you are' when something is handed over.
- 'Мо́жна меню́?' and 'Мо́жна раху́нок?' ask for the menu and for the bill.

examples.source: Can I have the menu, please?
Excuse me! Can I have the check?

culture.title: Eating out and eating together in Ukraine
culture.text:
'Смачно́го!' is heard far more often than its English equivalent. A waiter says it when bringing the food, friends say it as they start to eat, and people say it to a colleague they find eating lunch. The usual answer is 'Дя́кую!'.

In a café or restaurant the waiter brings the bill only when you ask for it, since bringing it earlier would seem to hurry the guests. Catch the waiter's eye or say 'Ви́бачте!', then 'Мо́жна раху́нок, будь ла́ска?'. A tip of about ten percent is usual when the service was good.

Borscht is the dish most closely tied to Ukraine: a soup of beets and other vegetables, often cooked with meat, with as many versions as there are regions and families. It is served with sour cream, 'смета́на', and often with small garlic bread rolls called 'пампу́шки'. In 2022 UNESCO added the culture of cooking Ukrainian borscht to its list of intangible cultural heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.

Varenyky are half-moons of dough around a filling, boiled and served with sour cream or fried onion. The most common fillings are:

- potatoes, 'карто́пля'
- the fresh curd cheese 'сир'
- cabbage
- cherries, for a sweet dish

Coffee has its own tradition, above all in Lviv, a city known for its many coffee houses, where 'ка́ва' is as much a reason to meet as a drink.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
Which word names a cup?
exercises.explanation: 'Ча́шка' is a cup and 'скля́нка' a drinking glass; 'раху́нок' is the bill and 'ковбаса́' is sausage.

exercises.prompt: The waiter brings your food. What do you say to your friends?
exercises.explanation: 'Смачно́го!' wishes everyone a good meal and is said when food is served or someone starts to eat.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Смачно́го!' say word for word?
exercises.explanation: It is the genitive of 'смачни́й'. A wish puts what is wished in the genitive, and the words for 'I wish you' and the noun the adjective describes are left out.

choices: Can I have the menu, please?
Can I have the check, please?
Can I have some water, please?

exercises.prompt: Which question asks about a direct object that is a person?
exercises.explanation: 'Кого́?' is the accusative question for people and animals, and 'що?' is the question for things. 'Хто?' asks about the subject, and 'де?' asks where.
The coffee is the direct object, and a feminine noun in '-а' changes it to '-у' in the accusative.
A feminine noun in '-а' takes '-у' in the accusative, whether it names a person or a thing.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'суп' stay the same in 'Я хо́чу суп'?
choices: Masculine nouns that name things have the same form in the nominative and the accusative
Every masculine noun keeps its form in the accusative
exercises.explanation: Only masculine nouns that name people or animals take '-а' or '-я'. A soup is a thing, so 'суп' keeps its form.
A waiter is a person, so the masculine noun adds '-а' after its hard final consonant.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'Андрі́й' completes 'Я зна́ю...', 'I know Andrii'?
exercises.explanation: Andrii is a person, and a masculine noun ending in 'й' takes '-я' in the accusative. 'Андрі́ю' is the vocative, used to call him.

exercises.hint_source: Oksana knows the teacher, a man.
exercises.explanation: 'Вчи́тель' names a person and ends in a soft 'ль', so its accusative adds '-я'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Окса́ну ба́чить Тара́с', who sees whom?
choices: Oksana and Taras see someone else.
exercises.explanation: 'Окса́ну' has the accusative ending '-у', so she is the object, and 'Тара́с' is the subject. Putting the subject last makes it the new information: 'It is Taras who sees Oksana'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'кіт' become 'кота́' in 'Я ба́чу кота́'?
choices: The stress mark changes the vowel
A cat is an animal, so the masculine noun takes '-а', and the opened syllable brings back the 'о' of the root
exercises.explanation: Animate masculine nouns take '-а' in the accusative. The ending opens the syllable, so the 'і' of the closed syllable in 'кіт' returns to 'о'.

exercises.prompt: Match each accusative pronoun with its English meaning

exercises.explanation: The accusative of 'я' is 'мене́'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Я ба́чу її́ бра́та' mean?
choices: I see her and her brother.
exercises.explanation: A noun follows 'її́', so here it means 'her', saying whose brother it is, and 'бра́та' is the object.

exercises.prompt: In 'Як тебе́ зва́ти?', what is 'тебе́'?
choices: The accusative of 'ти': the person who is called by a name
The nominative of 'ти': the subject of the sentence
The vocative of 'ти': the person spoken to
exercises.explanation: 'Зва́ти' means 'to call', and the sentence has no subject. Literally it is 'how you to-call?', with the person named as the object of the calling.
The adjective agrees with 'ка́ву', a feminine noun in the accusative, so its '-а' also becomes '-у'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I know your new friend', for a friend who is a man, said to someone you call 'ти'?
exercises.explanation: The friend is a man and the object, so the possessive, the adjective and the noun all take the animate masculine accusative: 'твого́ ново́го дру́га'.
'Мо́ва' is feminine and in the accusative, 'мо́ву', so the adjective changes '-а' to '-у' as well.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'п’ю' written with an apostrophe?
choices: It shows that a letter is silent
It keeps the 'п' hard and the [j] of 'ю' sounded separately
exercises.explanation: The 'и' of 'пи́ти' drops out, and the ending begins with [j]. The 'п' is never fully soft, so the apostrophe keeps it hard and the [j] separate: [pju].

exercises.prompt: How is the 'в' of 'ковбаса́' said?
choices: [ʋ], because it comes before a vowel
It is not said at all
[w], as in 'cow', because it ends a syllable before a consonant
exercises.explanation: 'В' is [ʋ] before a vowel and [w] at the end of a syllable before a consonant, here before 'б'.
The 'ти' form of 'пи́ти' is 'п’єш', with the apostrophe after 'п'.
The 'вони́' form of 'ї́сти' is 'їдя́ть', which shows the 'д' of the old stem.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'хоті́ти' goes with 'вони́'?
exercises.explanation: 'Хоті́ти' has the stem 'хоч-' and first conjugation endings, and the 'вони́' ending is '-уть'.

exercises.hint_source: What do you want? (to two friends)
exercises.explanation: Two people are addressed with 'ви', and its form of 'хоті́ти' is 'хо́чете'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Я хо́чу ї́сти' usually mean?
exercises.explanation: Literally it is 'I want to-eat', the everyday way to say 'I am hungry'. 'Я хо́чу пи́ти.' says 'I am thirsty'.

exercises.prompt: 'Вода́' is stressed on the last syllable, but 'Я п’ю во́ду' stresses the first. Why?
choices: Ukrainian stress is free and can move between forms of a word, so it is learned with each form
The accusative always moves the stress to the first syllable
exercises.explanation: No rule predicts the move: 'сестра́' keeps its stress in 'сестру́', while 'вода́' becomes 'во́ду'. Learn the stress with each form.

exercises.prompt: Which word is a predicative word?
exercises.explanation: 'Мо́жна' is the whole predicate of a sentence with no subject. 'Ду́же' is an adverb, 'смачни́й' an adjective and 'раху́нок' a noun.

exercises.prompt: In 'Мо́жна ка́ву?', why is 'ка́ву' in the accusative?
choices: 'Мо́жна' is a verb that takes the nominative
Every noun in a question is in the accusative
It is the thing you ask to be given, the object of a giving that is understood but not said
exercises.explanation: The sentence asks for coffee to be given, so the coffee is treated as a direct object.

exercises.hint_source: Can I have a glass, please?
exercises.explanation: The thing asked for after 'мо́жна' is in the accusative, so 'скля́нка' becomes 'скля́нку'.

exercises.prompt: What is 'мені́' in 'Мені́ борщ, будь ла́ска'?
choices: A form of 'я' in the dative, 'to-me', the person something is given to
exercises.explanation: The accusative of 'я' is 'мене́'. 'Мені́' is the dative, learned whole in this phrase for now.

exercises.prompt_source: Can I have the check, please?
And tea with sugar for me, please.

exercises.explanation: Taras is a person, so the masculine noun takes '-а'.
The 'вона́' form of 'пи́ти' is 'п’є', and 'вода́' becomes 'во́ду', with the stress moved.
The 'ми' form of 'ї́сти' is 'їмо́', and plural things keep their form in the accusative.
'Мені́..., будь ла́ска' is the fixed way to order, and 'борщ' names a thing, so it keeps its form.

exercises.prompt_source: Do you know my sister? (to a friend)
exercises.explanation: Both the possessive and the noun take the feminine accusative: 'мою́ сестру́'.

exercises.prompt_source: Sam is reading an interesting book.
exercises.explanation: 'Кни́га' is the direct object, so it becomes 'кни́гу', and the adjective agrees with it: 'ціка́ва' becomes 'ціка́ву'.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb form with its meaning
